title: Formula 1
description: Start with the top rung of single-seater racing: a world championship where constructors design cars inside a tight rulebook and drivers race them wheel to wheel. The season began in 1950, and the format still follows the same spine of practice, qualifying, and a grand prix distance. What decides races is rarely speed alone; it is tyre life, pit timing, and the choice of when to attack or defend. A driver who manages tyres well can win from behind, while a driver who burns them early fades late. That blend of engineering, fitness, and racecraft is what makes this class the reference point for the rest of motorsport.

topics.History: The championship traces to 1950 and to grand prix racing before it. Over the decades the cars changed shape, but the spine of practice, qualifying, and a set-distance race stayed.
topics.Rules: A strict technical rulebook limits what teams may build, so the contest is about design within limits. Qualifying orders the grid, and points reward the top ten finishers.
topics.Techniques: Winning calls for tyre management, well-timed stops, and clean overtaking. Drivers study braking points and exit speed because a tenth gained at a corner exit pays off down the whole straight.
topics.Safety: Cockpit protection, crash structures, protective clothing, and circuit barriers all work together, and races are supported by marshals and medical crews.

demo.code:
LAPS = 58
LAP_KM = 5.412
print("Example grand prix distance")
print("Laps: %d, lap length: %.3f km" % (LAPS, LAP_KM))
print("Race distance: %.1f km" % (LAPS * LAP_KM))
print("Pit stop example: 2 stops at 22 seconds = %d seconds in the pits" % (2 * 22))
print("Points for a win: 25")
demo.expected_output:
Example grand prix distance
Laps: 58, lap length: 5.412 km
Race distance: 313.9 km
Pit stop example: 2 stops at 22 seconds = 44 seconds in the pits
Points for a win: 25

title: NASCAR
description: Picture a full field of heavy stock cars racing inches apart on an oval for hundreds of miles. That is the heart of this discipline, which dates to 1948. The slipstream matters enormously: a car tucked behind another goes faster with less effort, so drivers work in packs and time their moves. Long races punish impatience, and a late caution can throw the whole order open again. Pit crews decide races too, since a fast stop for fuel and tyres can gain positions that no amount of speed on track can buy back.

topics.History: The series began in 1948 and grew from regional stock car racing into a national headline series, keeping its oval-racing identity as it added road courses.
topics.Rules: A set race distance, caution restarts, and pit strategy shape every event. Late cautions can erase leads, so the closing laps often decide the result.
topics.Techniques: Drivers draft to gain speed, save tyres on long runs, and pick pit moments carefully. Racing in a pack demands steady hands and constant awareness of the cars around.
topics.Safety: Roll cages, restraint systems, protective clothing, and barrier design protect drivers in heavy contact, and safety crews stand ready at every track.

demo.code:
CARS = 40
DRAFT_GAIN_MPH = 4
print("Drafting example")
print("Cars in the field: %d" % CARS)
print("Lead car speed: 190 mph, drafting car gain: %d mph" % DRAFT_GAIN_MPH)
print("Drafting car speed: %d mph" % (190 + DRAFT_GAIN_MPH))
print("Pit stop example: fuel and four tyres in about 12 seconds")
demo.expected_output:
Drafting example
Cars in the field: 40
Lead car speed: 190 mph, drafting car gain: 4 mph
Drafting car speed: 194 mph
Pit stop example: fuel and four tyres in about 12 seconds

title: IndyCar
description: American open-wheel racing at its fastest lives here, crowned by a 500-mile classic first run in 1911. The calendar mixes ovals, road courses, and street circuits, which is what makes the championship so demanding: a driver must be brave and precise on a high-speed oval one weekend and delicate under braking on a street track the next. Pit strategy and fuel saving decide many races, and a well-timed boost or a clean restart can move a driver several places at once. No single skill wins this championship; versatility does.

topics.History: The story starts with a 500-mile race in 1911 that became a national institution. The modern series keeps that race as its centrepiece and adds road and street rounds.
topics.Rules: A shared chassis keeps costs in check while teams tune aerodynamics and setup. Boosts, pit stops, and restarts all shape race outcomes.
topics.Techniques: Versatility is the core skill: high-speed oval discipline, road-course braking, and street-circuit accuracy, plus fuel and tyre management everywhere.
topics.Safety: Cockpit protection, crash structures, restraint systems, and safer barriers protect drivers at very high speeds.

demo.code:
SPEED_MPH = 230
KMH = SPEED_MPH * 1.60934
print("Oval speed conversion")
print("%d mph = %.1f km/h" % (SPEED_MPH, KMH))
print("Push-to-pass example: 200 seconds of boost per race, used in bursts")
print("Pit stops in a 500-mile race: typically 6 to 8")
demo.expected_output:
Oval speed conversion
230 mph = 370.1 km/h
Push-to-pass example: 200 seconds of boost per race, used in bursts
Pit stops in a 500-mile race: typically 6 to 8

title: World Rally Championship
description: Rallying is racing against the clock on real roads, and its world championship dates to 1973. Crews tackle timed stages on gravel, snow, ice, and asphalt, linked by road sections driven at legal speeds. The co-driver is the second half of the team: their pace notes call every corner and crest before the driver sees it, so the car can run flat out on unfamiliar roads. Cars take a beating, crews fix damage against the clock, and conditions change stage by stage. It is the most complete test of driver, navigator, and machine in motorsport.

topics.History: The championship began in 1973, formalising a sport that grew from long road rallies into a calendar of events on every surface and in every season.
topics.Rules: Timed stages decide the result, road sections link them, and service time is limited, so crews must repair damage fast or carry it.
topics.Techniques: Pace notes are the key skill: the co-driver calls the road ahead and the driver commits to it. Grip management on gravel, snow, and ice decides stage times.
topics.Safety: Roll cages, fire systems, harnesses, helmets, and closed stages protect crews, and spectators are kept behind marked lines.

demo.code:
STAGE_KM = 24.6
TIME_MIN = 14.5
print("Stage average speed")
print("Stage length: %.1f km, time: %.1f minutes" % (STAGE_KM, TIME_MIN))
print("Average speed: %.1f km/h" % (STAGE_KM / (TIME_MIN / 60.0)))
print("Service halt example: 45 minutes to repair and reset the car")
demo.expected_output:
Stage average speed
Stage length: 24.6 km, time: 14.5 minutes
Average speed: 101.8 km/h
Service halt example: 45 minutes to repair and reset the car

title: Motocross
description: Dirt, jumps, and forty riders charging into the first corner: that is motocross. Events run two motos, and the overall result rewards the rider who is strong in both, not just one. The start decides a lot, since passing on a narrow, rutted track is hard work. But the deeper skill is riding a changing circuit: ruts deepen, berms break down, and the fast line moves lap by lap. Fitness matters as much as bravery, because a moto at full effort is one of the most physically demanding races in motorsport.

topics.History: The sport grew from off-road scrambling into a global championship, keeping its dirt-circuit identity while bikes and tracks became far more specialised.
topics.Rules: Two-moto formats reward consistency. Starts are gated, course limits are marked, and penalties cover jump starts and cutting the course.
topics.Techniques: A fast start, clean jumping, and smooth cornering through berms and ruts win races. Riders read the track as it changes and adjust lines every lap.
topics.Safety: Helmets, boots, armour, and goggles are standard, tracks are prepared before racing, and medical cover is present at every meeting.

demo.code:
LAP_SECONDS = 118
print("Motocross lap average")
print("Example lap: %d seconds" % LAP_SECONDS)
print("Laps in a 30-minute moto at this pace: %.1f" % (30 * 60 / LAP_SECONDS))
print("Jumps per lap example: 12, taken at full throttle on the fastest line")
demo.expected_output:
Motocross lap average
Example lap: 118 seconds

title: Endurance Racing
description: The question in endurance racing is not who is fastest for one lap, but who is still fast at hour twenty. The classic is a 24-hour race first run in 1923, and the format has spread to six- and twelve-hour events. Drivers share a car in stints, handing over at pit stops while the crew works. Faster and slower classes share the track, so traffic management is a skill in itself. Night, rain, and tiredness all bite late in a race, and the teams that win are the ones that plan fuel, tyres, and driver changes like a military operation.

topics.History: Endurance racing grew from the 1923 Le Mans 24-hour race into a worldwide discipline, keeping the same test: distance covered against the clock.
topics.Rules: A set time limit, limited driver stints, and shared classes define the format. Pit work and reliability count as heavily as lap times.
topics.Techniques: Crews plan stints, fuel loads, and tyre changes hours ahead. Drivers manage traffic, darkness, and fatigue while keeping pace.
topics.Safety: Crash structures, fire systems, cooling, and round-the-clock medical cover protect drivers through night and changing weather.

demo.code:
DISTANCE_KM = 5200
HOURS = 24
print("Endurance distance example")
print("Distance covered: %d km in %d hours" % (DISTANCE_KM, HOURS))
print("Average speed including stops: %.1f km/h" % (DISTANCE_KM / HOURS))
print("Pit stops example: 32 stops at 60 seconds = %d minutes in the pits" % (32 * 60 // 60))
demo.expected_output:
Endurance distance example
Distance covered: 5200 km in 24 hours
Average speed including stops: 216.7 km/h
Pit stops example: 32 stops at 60 seconds = 32 minutes in the pits

title: Karting
description: Almost every professional driver started here, in a small kart on a short circuit. Karts are simple machines, which is exactly the point: with no suspension to hide mistakes, a driver learns lines, braking, and racecraft in their purest form. Races are short, fields are big, and overtaking happens constantly. Costs stay far below car racing, so karting is the doorway into the sport for most young drivers. It is also a complete sport in its own right, with its own championships and a fiercely competitive senior scene.

topics.History: Karting began in the late 1950s as a low-cost way to race, and it became the standard first step for drivers heading to car racing.
topics.Rules: Age and engine classes keep competition fair. Heats lead to finals, and officials penalise avoidable contact and course cutting.
topics.Techniques: Because karts are simple, they teach the fundamentals cleanly: lines, braking, smooth inputs, and reading the driver ahead.
topics.Safety: Helmets, suits, gloves, and rib protection are standard, and karts are fitted with bumpers and guards.

demo.code:
TRACK_M = 1100
LAP_SECONDS = 54
print("Kart average speed")
print("Track length: %d m, lap time: %d seconds" % (TRACK_M, LAP_SECONDS))
print("Average speed: %.1f km/h" % (TRACK_M / LAP_SECONDS * 3.6))
print("Practice laps in a 10-minute session: about %d" % (10 * 60 // LAP_SECONDS))
demo.expected_output:
Kart average speed
Track length: 1100 m, lap time: 54 seconds
Average speed: 73.3 km/h
Practice laps in a 10-minute session: about 11

title: Drag Racing
description: Two cars, one straight strip, and a race over in seconds: drag racing strips the sport down to launch and acceleration. The start lights decide much of it, because a slow reaction cannot be recovered over a quarter mile. The fastest machines cover that distance in under four seconds, which demands enormous power and precise traction control. There is no strategy to hide behind and no corner to make up time in; the run is won or lost at the tree and in the first sixty feet. That brutal simplicity is the whole appeal.

topics.History: The sport grew from street contests into organised racing with professional classes, keeping the same format: two cars, one strip, first to the line.
topics.Rules: Pairs race a set distance, usually a quarter mile. The start lights govern the launch, and foul starts cost the run.
topics.Techniques: Reaction at the lights, traction off the line, and clean shifts decide everything. The first sixty feet often decide the whole run.
topics.Safety: Roll cages, fire systems, parachutes, protective clothing, and long shutdown areas protect drivers at extreme speeds.

demo.code:

RUN_S = 4.2
print("Reaction time example")
print("Reaction: %.2f seconds, run: %.1f seconds" % (REACTION_S, RUN_S))
print("Total from lights to finish: %.2f seconds" % (REACTION_S + RUN_S))
print("A 0.10 second slower reaction loses about 0.10 seconds at the finish")
demo.expected_output:
Reaction time example
Reaction: 0.15 seconds, run: 4.2 seconds
Total from lights to finish: 4.35 seconds
A 0.10 second slower reaction loses about 0.10 seconds at the finish

title: Touring Cars
description: Touring cars are the cars in the showroom, turned into racers. That familiarity is the point: fans watch the same models they drive, racing bumper to bumper. Fields are big, contact is frequent, and sprint formats with several races per meeting mean no single result decides a weekend. Weight penalties for winners and reversed grids in some series keep the pack tight. The driving style is aggressive but controlled, because a driver who wrecks rivals soon finds rivals returning the favour.

topics.History: The discipline grew from production-car racing into major national series, keeping its identity: recognisable cars, big fields, close racing.
topics.Rules: Production-based cars, sprint formats, and balance measures such as success ballast keep results unpredictable.
topics.Techniques: Drivers race door to door, defend lines, and overtake under braking, all while keeping the car intact for the next race of the meeting.
topics.Safety: Roll cages, fire systems, harnesses, and protective clothing protect drivers in frequent contact.

demo.code:
BALLAST_KG = 60
LAP_SECONDS = 95
print("Success ballast example")
print("Winner ballast: %d kg" % BALLAST_KG)
print("Lap time without ballast: %d seconds" % LAP_SECONDS)
print("Estimated lap time with ballast: %.1f seconds" % (LAP_SECONDS + BALLAST_KG * 0.03))
demo.expected_output:
Success ballast example
Winner ballast: 60 kg
Lap time without ballast: 95 seconds
Estimated lap time with ballast: 96.8 seconds

title: Superbike Racing
description: Take a road superbike, prepare it for racing, and put twenty of them on a circuit: that is superbike racing. The bikes are fast, the lean angles are extreme, and the packs stay tight because slipstreaming works so well on straights. Electronics help with traction, but they do not ride the bike; throttle feel, braking courage, and body position still decide races. Setup is a constant conversation between rider and team, since a small suspension change can turn a nervous bike into a winning one. Lead changes come thick and fast.

topics.History: The world championship grew from production racing into a headline motorcycle series, keeping road-based machines at its core.
topics.Rules: Production-based bikes, multiple races per weekend, and a points scale decide the championship.
topics.Techniques: Lean angle, braking, throttle feel, and slipstreaming decide positions. Riders give precise setup feedback after every session.
topics.Safety: Helmets, airbag leathers, boots, gloves, air fences, and gravel traps protect riders at high speed.

demo.code:
RACES = 3
WINS = 2
print("Superbike weekend example")
print("Races: %d, wins: %d" % (RACES, WINS))
print("Win rate: %.1f%%" % (WINS / RACES * 100.0))
print("Points example: two wins at 25 points = %d points" % (2 * 25))
demo.expected_output:
Superbike weekend example
Races: 3, wins: 2
Win rate: 66.7%
Points example: two wins at 25 points = 50 points

title: Speedway
description: No brakes, one gear, four laps, and a bike sliding sideways through every corner: speedway is motorsport stripped to its essentials. Heats score 3, 2, 1, and 0, and team meetings stack heat after heat into a full evening. Riders steer with the throttle, balancing a sliding rear wheel against the dirt's grip. Gate starts matter hugely, since passing on a short oval is hard. The dirt changes through the night, so the rider who reads the surface wins. It is short, loud, and completely rider-dependent.

topics.History: Speedway grew from 1920s dirt-track racing into a team sport with leagues in several countries, keeping its four-lap heat format.
topics.Rules: Four riders, four laps, points 3-2-1-0. Team meetings are built from a programme of heats.
topics.Techniques: Riders slide with the throttle, launch hard from the gate, and hunt for grip as the dirt surface changes.
topics.Safety: Helmets, leathers, boots, gloves, and air fences protect riders, and meetings are run under strict start procedures.

demo.code:
LAPS = 4
LAP_SECONDS = 15
print("Speedway heat example")
print("Laps: %d, lap time: %d seconds" % (LAPS, LAP_SECONDS))
print("Heat time: %d seconds" % (LAPS * LAP_SECONDS))
print("Heats in an evening: 15, total race time about %d minutes" % (15 * LAPS * LAP_SECONDS // 60))
demo.expected_output:
Speedway heat example
Laps: 4, lap time: 15 seconds
Heat time: 60 seconds
Heats in an evening: 15, total race time about 15 minutes

title: Drifting
description: Drifting is the art of controlled sliding, judged rather than timed. Drivers throw the car sideways and hold the slide through corner after corner, scored on line, angle, speed, and style. Qualifying runs are solo, but the heart of the sport is the tandem battle: a lead car sets the run and a chase car must follow it door to door, mirroring every slide. Cars are rear-wheel-drive, tuned for power and lock, and drivers steer as much with the throttle as with the wheel. Commitment wins: the best runs are fast, sideways, and millimetres from the markers.

topics.History: The sport grew from Japanese road driving into judged competition with series worldwide, keeping its scoring on line, angle, speed, and style.
topics.Rules: Qualifying is solo; battles are tandem, with a lead car and a chase car judged against each other.
topics.Techniques: Slides are started with handbrake, clutch, or weight transfer, then held with throttle and steering. Chase drivers must match the lead car closely.
topics.Safety: Roll cages, fire systems, harnesses, and barriered courses protect drivers, and each run is marshalled.

ANGLE_DEG = 42
SPEED_KMH = 95
print("Drift run example")
print("Slide angle: %d degrees, entry speed: %d km/h" % (ANGLE_DEG, SPEED_KMH))
print("Style score example: line 9, angle 9, speed 8 = %d of 30" % (9 + 9 + 8))
demo.expected_output:
Drift run example
Slide angle: 42 degrees, entry speed: 95 km/h

title: Off-Road Racing
description: Desert racing is navigation, endurance, and survival as much as speed. The flagship event dates to 1979 and runs over many days, with timed stages across sand, rock, and dry riverbeds linked by liaison sections. Crews navigate by roadbook, manage fuel and tyres far from help, and repair damage in the dust. The vehicles are built to take punishment: prototypes, production-based cars, and racing trucks all share the same brutal terrain. One wrong turn or one broken part can cost hours, so the winners are usually the crews that make the fewest mistakes, not the fastest ones.

topics.History: Cross-country rallying grew around the Dakar event of 1979 into a world discipline, keeping the multi-day, multi-terrain format.
topics.Rules: Timed stages plus liaison sections, roadbook navigation, and penalties for missed waypoints define the format.
topics.Techniques: Navigation accuracy, sand and rock driving, and tyre and fuel management matter more than outright speed.
topics.Safety: Roll cages, fire systems, tracking, helmets, and helicopter rescue cover crews in remote terrain.

STAGE_KM = 350

print("Days: %d, average stage: %d km" % (DAYS, STAGE_KM))
print("Total stage distance: %d km" % (DAYS * STAGE_KM))
print("Tyres example: 2 spares carried per stage")

Multi-day rally example

title: Hillclimb
description: One car, one hill, one run against the clock: hillclimb is the purest time trial in motorsport. Courses run from sub-minute sprints to mountain roads several kilometres long, mixing hairpins, sweepers, and surface changes. Every kind of car competes, from road cars to winged prototypes built only for hills. With no traffic and no slipstream, the result is driver, machine, and gradient alone. A single error ruins a run, so the winners are the drivers who commit fully yet never overstep. It is short, intense, and spectacular.

topics.History: Hillclimbing dates to the early twentieth century and remains one of the oldest timed motorsports, run on hills worldwide.
topics.Rules: Solo timed runs decide the result, with practice runs first and the fastest timed run counting.
topics.Techniques: Learning the hill, braking late but cleanly, and carrying speed through fast sections win runs. Setup must suit the gradient.
topics.Safety: Roll cages, fire systems, barriers, marshals, and medical cover protect drivers and spectators.

TIME_S = 78.5
print("Hillclimb average speed")

print("Average speed: %.1f km/h" % (COURSE_M / TIME_S * 3.6))
print("Gradient example: 120 m climb over 1850 m = %.1f%% average" % (120 / 1850 * 100.0))
demo.expected_output:
Hillclimb average speed

title: Powerboat Racing
description: Motorsport on water moves at the same speeds as on land, with none of the grip. Formula 1 powerboats ride tunnel hulls on a cushion of air and pass 200 kilometres per hour on buoy-marked circuits. The water itself is the challenge: wind chop, wakes, and changing trim all move the boat under the driver, who adjusts constantly. Races start rolling behind a pace boat and run a set lap count. Safety capsules and rescue teams are central, because a crash on water at speed leaves no run-off. It is fast, wet, and unforgiving.

topics.History: The sport grew from early speedboat contests into world championships, with tunnel-hull Formula 1 boats as the fastest class.
topics.Rules: Buoy circuits, rolling starts, and set lap counts define races, with penalties for buoy and start infringements.
topics.Techniques: Drivers read chop and wakes, trim the boat, and pick lines that keep the hull stable at speed.
topics.Safety: Safety capsules, harnesses, helmets, life jackets, and rescue cover protect drivers on water.

demo.code:
SPEED_KMH = 220
LAP_MIN = 1.2
print("Powerboat lap example")
print("Top speed: %d km/h, lap time: %.1f minutes" % (SPEED_KMH, LAP_MIN))
print("Distance per lap at top speed for 1.2 minutes: %.1f km" % (SPEED_KMH * LAP_MIN / 60.0))
demo.expected_output:
Powerboat lap example
Top speed: 220 km/h, lap time: 1.2 minutes

title: Truck Racing
description: Five-tonne racing trucks, door to door on a circuit: truck racing is the heavyweight division of circuit racing. The headline series runs in Europe, with production-based cabs on racing chassis and powerful turbocharged engines. Brakes are water-cooled to cope with the weight, and sprint formats give several races per weekend. The sight of such huge machines leaning through corners and braking hard is the draw, but the racing itself is disciplined, with strict contact rules. Fans recognise the trucks from the road, which makes the spectacle feel close to home.

topics.History: The sport grew from truck competitions into a European championship, keeping production-based cabs and sprint formats.
topics.Rules: Weight and engine rules, sprint races, and strict contact rules define the series.
topics.Techniques: Drivers manage braking distances, weight transfer, and heat in brakes and tyres while racing closely.
topics.Safety: Roll cages, fire systems, harnesses, and barriered circuits protect drivers in heavy vehicles.
